gates.reasoning: Technical terms that the lesson uses (RAG, embedding, vector store, retrieval) are defined at or before their first use with simple language and analogies. Definitions do not rely on undefined jargon.

The lesson omits several of the five core concepts required: it does not explain RAG's handling of private data, nor does it cover chunking, the indexing vs querying phases, augmentation (inserting retrieved text into the prompt), or the generation step (model producing an answer from augmented prompt).
gates.evidence: Imagine you have a very smart student. This student knows a lot of general information. But sometimes, you ask a question about a very specific topic. The student might not know the exact answer. They might even make up an answer that sounds right but is wrong. This is like a computer model. It knows general things, but not every specific detail from every book in the world.
gates.fix_instruction: Add clear, separate short paragraphs that explicitly cover each of the five required concepts: (1) the three problems RAG solves (knowledge cutoff, private/company data access, hallucination) with brief examples for each; (2) embeddings and that they are produced by a separate embedding model; (3) the vector store plus chunking and how indexing works offline; (4) augmentation — how retrieved chunks are inserted into the model prompt with an instruction to use only that context; and (5) generation — the model reading the augmented prompt and producing an answer (and citing sources). Keep each explanation simple and label them so a beginner can find them.

summary: The lesson is clear and simply written and correctly explains embeddings and retrieval at a basic level, but it misses several essential RAG components. To be usable by a beginner, add the missing core concepts (private data, chunking, indexing vs querying, augmentation, generation) and one concrete end-to-end worked example.
